claim: A chiropractor's use of a self-created credential designation in advertisements is inherently misleading and therefore afforded no First Amendment protection, and a chiropractor's failure to clearly identify himself as a chiropractor in advertisements using one of the four designated terms prescribed by regulation violates the applicable administrative code, but a corresponding violation of Fourteenth Amendment due process rights nonetheless occurs where the notice letter, even if it alleged the designation was "misleading," failed to specify which particular administrative code provisions were implicated, regardless of whether the chiropractor had a full and fair opportunity to present a defense.
initial_reasoning: The citation 2019 Ohio 3243 directly contradicts the claim that a chiropractor's failure to clearly identify himself as a chiropractor in advertisements using one of the four designated terms prescribed by regulation violates the applicable administrative code. The citation specifically states that a plain, common sense reading of Ohio Adm. Code 4734-9-02(F) and (G) in pari materia leads to the conclusion that the board intended that to comply with Ohio Adm.Code 4734-9-02(F), a chiropractic physician may "clearly reveal" himself or herself in advertisements only by using one of the four designated terms set forth in Adm.Code 4734-9-02(G). This directly supports the judgment in the cited case, which overruled the third assignment of error, that the common pleas court did not abuse its discretion in determining that there was reliable, probative, and substantial evidence to support the board's finding that appellant's use of the designation D.C. did not clearly identify him as a chiropractor in his print and television advertisements in violation of Ohio Adm.Code 4734-9-02(F).
